The dispatcher claims a handle-keyed call only for handles in its own range, so the three back ends never contend; path-keyed calls (F_OPEN, F_STAT, F_OPENDIR, F_CHDIR, F_GETCWD, F_GETFREE, M_GETDATE, and the write calls F_UNLINK, F_RENAME, F_MKDIR, F_RMDIR, F_TRUNCATE, F_CHMOD) it claims outright, since with a root there is exactly one volume; F_FTRUNCATE is handle-keyed and follows the handle rule. The one interaction worth knowing: with a root configured, the extended-NEX bridge's sibling lookup is skipped, so only the NEX's own filename still resolves beside the NEX — otherwise one name could mean two files.

Reading the filespec. Two readers, and the distinction is load-bearing. A dot command's COMMAND TAIL is "terminated by $00, $0d or ':'" (readdir.asm:78-79), so M_EXECCMD uses read_cmdline. A FILESPEC is NUL-terminated and nothing else — every esxDOS header block says so in those words — so the four path-keyed calls plus the two pre-existing F_OPEN sites use read_filespec. Applying the command-tail terminator set to a filespec truncates exactly the drive-qualified form the API is built around: F_OPEN is documented as "A=drive specifier (overridden if filespec includes a drive)", esxapi.def:129-130 assigns '*' and '$' as drive letters, and NextZXOS's ROM carries literals like "c:/nextzxos/autoexec.1st". That bug shipped into review: one shared helper split on ':', so "c:/hello.txt" reached resolve() as the single byte "c" and every drive-qualified open returned ENOENT. HFS-84..88 pin all four calls through the dispatcher and HFS-89 pins that M_EXECCMD still splits.

A bad root is fatal. EsxdosHostFs::validate_root() is called from main.cpp beside the --rzx-record start-up check, and a root that does not exist or is not a directory exits non-zero. It has to: parsing the flag also sets esxdos_stub, so continuing would quietly serve the in-memory file and a typo in a CI script would go green with the feature off. configure() calls the same function, so the two cannot disagree.

Containment. Primary confinement is LEXICAL and consults nothing: the guest path is split, . dropped, .. popped, and a pop that would leave the root refused. An escaping path is therefore never constructed. The code is the one real NextZXOS gives, which treats .. above the root as a name missing from the root directory: esx_enotdir when more path follows, for every call. A bare .. is, per call, what a missing last name is: esx_enoent for lookups (F_STAT included), esx_einval for a create, esx_enotdir for F_OPENDIR and F_CHDIR; resolve() returns the internal marker kBareDotDot (not an esxDOS code) for it and each call maps it. A guest absolute path is absolute within the root. Both / and \ separate components, on every host: FAT forbids a backslash inside a name, and treating it as an ordinary character would leave std::filesystem::path re-splitting it on a Windows build but not a POSIX one, so the lexical walk would enforce different things per platform. The drive qualifiers *:, $: and c: (esxapi.def:129-130) all map to the root. On top of that, every existing component is checked with symlink_status() and refused if it is a link, the result is canonicalised and re-checked against the canonical root, and an open re-checks once more afterwards. Those layers are genuinely independent, and that has a consequence worth stating plainly: no row can prove any single symlink check is load-bearing, because neutralising one does not change the answer. A reviewer measured it — all seven neutralised at once still gave a green suite. What the rows pin instead is that no call surface has lost all its protection, once per surface, using a link whose target is INSIDE the root (the only case containment cannot catch): HFS-12 stat, HFS-90 open, HFS-91 opendir, HFS-92 chdir. For open and stat the discriminating mutation is symlink_status → status, because their is_regular_file gate implicitly refuses a link too; for opendir and chdir deleting the explicit check is enough. The full note is in esxdos_hostfs.cpp. The residual TOCTOU window is documented in the .cpp: closing it needs an openat(O_NOFOLLOW) walk with no portable form across the Linux, macOS and MinGW builds.

The write calls. unlink, rename, mkdir, rmdir, truncate, ftruncate and chmod on EsxdosHostFs, and M_GETERR in the dispatcher (its texts are esxdos_error_message() in esxdos_trace.h). There is no VHDL for them: NextZXOS is software, so the oracle is a PROBE, kept in the tree (test/00regression/esxdos-write-probe.py, the nex command writes the two NEX files), run under real NextZXOS booted in jnext on a scratch copy of the SD image, and the answers recorded in test/fixtures/esxdos-write-probe/nextzxos.txt with the image's sha256, M_DOSVERSION (2.09) and the sha256 of the probe NEX files in its header. Every rule in the code names the recorded group it came from. The generator's DIVERGE table lists each place jnext deliberately answers otherwise, with its reason. To re-measure: esxdos-write-probe-measure.sh (the fixture's README.md). The order of checks is the measured one: lookups and the checks that do not write first, then, on a write-protected root, esx_edevicebusy, then the host change.

What the measurements showed, in the places a reader would guess otherwise: on success A is whatever the register held (junk), so the probe masks it, and the dispatcher returns 0; F_UNLINK of a directory is success and deletes nothing; F_TRUNCATE with a wildcard truncates the first match; F_CHMOD's A_WRITE is the inverse of FAT's read-only bit, A_READ is inert, and hidden and system are set together, so only A_WRITE, A_READ and the archive bit set are served (everything else is esx_enosys: refused, not faked); a name with ", <, >, |, : is esx_einval in every call; a trailing dot is dropped; a renamed current directory keeps its old name in F_GETCWD on a card (jnext shows the new one); F_RENAME of an empty destination means the current directory. A file is read-only when its host write permission is absent (host_read_only(), from the permission bits, never from whether the OS would refuse: the gate runs as root); F_STAT, F_FSTAT, F_READDIR and F_OPEN agree. An open file of ours (is_open_file(), fs::equivalent) refuses F_UNLINK, F_RENAME and F_TRUNCATE before any host call, so Windows' own refusal never decides. The NEX file a kept-open NEX reads through the extended-NEX bridge is not one of ours and is not protected from deleting itself. F_RENAME refuses an existing destination before the host call (POSIX rename(2) and MinGW's replace it). A directory rename closes our streams under it, renames, reopens them under the new path on every host (so the reopen path is exercised on Linux too), rebases the file and directory handle paths, and moves the CWD with it.

Two structural fixes came with these calls, because deleting makes them dangerous. The 8.3 aliases are no longer renumbered on every listing: a FAT alias is fixed when the file is created, and a program that deleted LONGNA~1.TXT must not find LONGNA~2.TXT naming another file. list_host_dir() keeps the aliases it handed out per directory (aliases_, not in a snapshot: it follows host changes no rewind undoes), the first listing numbers in sorted order, a later one keeps them, forgets the vanished, reserves every kept alias of a name still there (and every native 8.3 name) BEFORE giving a new name the lowest free tail, so a newcomer that sorts first never takes an existing file's short name, and a name that is itself 8.3 always keeps it. unlink, rmdir and rename free the alias of the name that goes at once (forget_alias()), as a FAT volume does, so a name created next takes it. And resolve() no longer takes a name merely because the host answers to it: a component counts as present only when the directory LISTING holds it byte for byte (or by case, or by its 8.3 name); a name the host answers to that the listing does not (Windows' own short name, numbered by creation order; macOS's normalisation) is refused with esx_eacces, so it cannot reach a different file than the listing shows under it, and the guest's spelling is never stored as the current directory.

Rewind. An open std::fstream is not snapshottable, so save_state writes only (handle, is_dir, mode, position, path) per open handle plus the guest CWD, and load_state reopens from that. Reads therefore rewind exactly. Writes cannot — the host side effect already happened — which is the whole reason writes are behind a second flag. That covers every call above: a snapshot taken before an F_UNLINK or F_RENAME does not bring the file back, and restore() drops a handle whose file is gone (the open fails and the slot stays closed), so F_READ on it is esx_ebadf.

Exact answers, or refusals. A listing mode is served only where the answer is exactly NextZXOS's, and refused with esx_enosys everywhere else: a caller that asked for a filtered or sorted listing and silently got neither is worse off than one told no. What NextZXOS answers was measured with a probe NEX launched from its Browser, listing one directory in every mode:

  • esx_mode_sf_enable with no exclude bit and no esx_sf_sort_enable in C (C = $00, and $07: the sort-key and reverse bits are inert without sort_enable) is the plain listing, entry for entry. NXModPlayer opens every listing after its first with $B0 (sf_enable, wildcards, LFN; C = 0). Exclusion and sorting are refused.
  • The wildcard that filters is the one passed to F_READDIR, not F_OPENDIR's: opened *.TXT and read *.* the listing is complete, and the reverse is filtered. NextZXOS matches it against the 8.3 name (* lists only names with no extension), so *.* matches every entry. So F_OPENDIR accepts the wildcard bit, and readdir() serves *.* and refuses any other pattern. The bit travels in the rewind snapshot's mode byte.
  • F_OPENDIR returns C = 0 ("sort operation not completed") whatever C it was given.
  • esx_mode_use_header stays refused: a host file has no header.

"Exactly" governs WHICH listing modes are served, i.e. which entries a listing returns. Entry order (host-name sort, not FAT directory order), name spelling (the host's case: NextZXOS lists a lower-case 8.3 FAT name as A.TXT, the stub a.txt) and the attribute bits (read-only on a read-only mount, hidden for a leading-dot name) follow the host and cannot be reproduced from it; lookup is case-insensitive, so no path call is affected.

F_GETCWD answers in NextZXOS's form, C:/ then each component's 8.3 name and a / (C:/AAA/T/SUBDIR~1/ was measured for an LFN of "sub dir long"), and with A = $FF for the filespec in DE. Since the guest then builds paths out of 8.3 names, resolve() accepts an entry's 8.3 name (in any case) as well as its host name; the 8.3 synthesis follows FAT's basis-name rule, including stripping leading dots first (.git is GIT~1, .hidden is HIDDEN~1, as measured); list_host_dir() is the one place a listing and its short names are made, so F_READDIR, F_GETCWD and resolve() cannot disagree on one. The error codes for bad paths are NextZXOS's measured ones too: a missing or non-directory component before the last is esx_enotdir, as is a missing directory for F_OPENDIR and F_CHDIR; a missing last component of F_OPEN / F_STAT is esx_enoent; F_OPEN and F_STAT of a directory are esx_einval. M_P3DOS is not answered: it bridges into NextZXOS ROM entry points including IDE_SECTOR_READ, and a directory has no sectors.

SCOPE, and the measurement behind it. This serves programs that reach the filesystem through RST $08 — a directly loaded NEX, and dot commands. It does NOT serve NextZXOS's Browser, file selector, BASIC or loader. That was the load-bearing assumption of the whole design, and it was settled experimentally before any of this was built (2026-09-23), not inferred:

Run (same build, same image, --log-level esxdos=trace) calls in $85..$B1 Browser opened at C:/, descended into C:/DEMOS/, scrolled 0 .ls from the NextZXOS command line 76

The .ls run is the positive control — it is F_OPENDIR ×2, F_READDIR ×35, F_GETCWD ×2, F_READ ×6, M_P3DOS ×22 and more — so the instrument plainly can see directory traffic. The Browser, listing a directory on screen, produced none of it. NextZXOS carries its own SD/SPI driver and FAT code in enNextZX.rom and never asks $0008. Reaching it would need a synthetic FAT32 volume at the block layer, which the project declined (doc/design/TASK89-ESXDOS-HOST-FILESYSTEM.md §0.1 decision 5). The boundary is permanent, and the user-facing docs say so in --help, the man page and the user guide because the flag's name invites the opposite assumption.

Tests, write calls. HFW-01..121 and GETERR-01..06 in test/esxdos_stub/esxdos_write_rows.cpp (class level, then the dispatcher's registers, then rewind), every expected value a line of the recording or a declared divergence, each row's comment naming its group; HFW-130..134 in esxdos_symlink_test (no write call acts on a symlink); the regression row esxdos-write-func runs the probe NEX on a writable root and on a write-protected one and judges every line against the recording (and refuses a probe edited without re-measuring), esxdos-write-oracle-func runs it under real NextZXOS on a scratch copy of the SD image and requires the recording back exactly, so the fixture cannot silently stop being reproducible.

Tests. HFS-01..122 in test/esxdos_stub/esxdos_hostfs_rows.cpp (linked into esxdos_stub_test): the sandbox and the 8.3/timestamp synthesis against the class, every register convention through the real dispatcher. The regression row esxdos-hostfs-func runs a real guest program that opens, seeks to offset 6, reads and prints a real host file through RST $08, then probes the sandbox from inside the guest — with a control run, --esxdos-stub alone, whose implicit root holds no such file, that must not produce the content. NXROOT-01..12 in esxdos_stub_test and NXROOT-13 in esxdos_symlink_test pin the implicit root (the NEX's directory, an explicit root winning, no root without a NEX or without the stub, read-only and writable, following an in-place and a cold-boot load, ending at a soft reset, the kept-open NEX, a symlinked NEX); the regression row esxdos-nexdir-func runs the same guest program from the CLI with the root implicit (absolute and bare relative path), overridden, taken from a .zip and absent.

Known gaps. Without --esxdos-stub or --esxdos-stub-root a directly loaded program still cannot reach host files other than the kept-open NEX and its siblings, a NEX from an archive gets no directory, and the in-memory file still has no F_SEEK. M_DOSVERSION reports 1.94 without the host bridge. M_GETERR is answered for a directly loaded NEX and with a host root; B=0, which raises a BASIC error report on a Next, is not.

docs.title: RZX
docs.text:
RZX records a session, and it does so by recording inputs rather than pictures. The file holds an embedded snapshot of the machine at the start plus, for every frame that follows, the instruction count and every value the program read back from an IN. Playing it back re-runs the original code: jnext feeds the recorded values through the port-dispatch hook at the points the program asks for them, so the program takes exactly the path it took when the recording was made. The result is a very small file that reproduces a run exactly instead of showing you a video of it — which is also why an RZX is a good bug report, and why it only works at all if the emulator executes the same instructions in the same order both times.

rzx.h holds the format, rzx_player.* and rzx_recorder.* the two directions. The snapshot a recording embeds is an SZX on the 128K and +3 (SzxSaver — all eight banks and the paging ports) and an SNA on the 48K (SnaSaver::save(), where the CPU view IS the machine).

RECORDING IS REFUSED ON A NEXT — Emulator::rzx_refused_by_machine(), owner decision 2026-09-26, and the derivation with its measurements lives at that definition. In short, an RZX holds a classic-Spectrum snapshot AND a per-frame log of IN VALUES WITHOUT THE PORTS THEY CAME FROM, and a Next fails both halves. The snapshot: none of SNA, SZX or Z80 describes a Next, so a 48K SNA of one — which jnext embedded until this change — holds no NextREGs, Layer 2, tilemap, sprites or Copper, and a recording replayed correctly only when the program happened to redraw its display every frame. The log: because it stores values and not ports, the snapshot and the log must agree on the guest's exact sequence of port reads, and nothing can detect it when they do not. Embedding a .jns — the one format that CAN represent a Next — was built and measured against that: the replayed guest made two reads the recording never captured (0x00E3, 0x243B), every value was consumed two positions early, and the guest wedged in a HALT with IFF1 clear.

Two facts from that experiment are worth keeping, because nothing in the tree demonstrates them any more. First, a .jns restore is faithful enough to RUN and not bit-exact enough to REPLAY: at the first run_frame the CPU state matched the recording exactly and the same snapshot animates correctly under --load, yet from that identical PC the first port read differed. Do not assume .jns is replay-grade. Second, the DMA was outside the log: dma_.read_io was wired to port_.read(), which has no RZX hook, so a DMA port read was neither recorded nor replayed. It now goes through PortDispatch::guest_read(), the RZX-aware read the CPU's IN also takes (in() forwards to it). read() stays hook-free on purpose: it is also every tool's read — the debugger's port_in() — and a tool's read is not input. port_in() is refused (RefusedRzx) while an RZX records or plays, as port_out() is: it dispatches the live handler, and a port read's side effects (a UART RX pop, the SPI shift, a Multiface strobe) are a change to the machine no recording can carry. On the playback branch guest_read() still raises the I/O watchpoint and latches the CAP-EVT Port event, with the replayed value, for the CPU's read and the DMA's alike. The DMA keeps its own timing; the CPU's bus cycle (fuse_z80_readport()) is around in(), not in guest_read().

Replay then agrees with the recording only while the DMA makes the same reads in the same order, and it does, given the same machine: whether a slot is a DMA burst or a CPU instruction (step_one_instruction()), how many bytes a burst moves (Dma::execute_burst(): block length, prescaler, dma_delay, the bus handshake) and which port each read hits are all functions of emulated state, which the replay rebuilds from the snapshot and the logged values. jnext's player delimits frames by emulator frame, not by the fetch counter, and the counter counts only CPU instructions, so DMA reads land in the frame they happened in on both sides. The gap is the snapshot: SNA and SZX hold no DMA registers and no NextREGs, and playback's init() resets the DMA. A transfer programmed before the recording started therefore replays from a reset DMA and goes out of step — documented for users in the RZX section of the user guide. rzx-dma-func (fixture demo/rzx_dma_demo) and dma_test GH283-01..12 pin it.

Playing a Next recording an older jnext wrote is NOT refused: load_rzx() warns, names what the embedded snapshot cannot restore, and plays. The file is a fait accompli and there is something to see — a program living in the 48K view replays correctly, which is why this went unnoticed.

A command-line recording starts once the --load/--inject is in the machine (emulator_start_rzx_record_when_loaded()), so that snapshot is the loaded program. The tape ROM traps stand down while RZX records or plays — see the trap block in run_frame() — and a fast-load tape already attached is switched to real-time loading (Emulator::rzx_suspend_tape_traps()). On playback the embedded snapshot — SNA, SZX or Z80 — is parsed straight from the file's bytes by Emulator::load_snapshot_from_memory(), using the load_from_buffer() entry each of those loaders has beside its file-path load(); nothing is written to a temporary file. Every way of starting a playback reaches load_rzx() on a freshly initialised machine whose EmulatorConfig::load_file is the recording — --rzx-play sets it as --load does, and the GUI's Play RZX item goes through MainWindow::handle_load_path() and the frontend cold boot like File > Load NEX File… — because that field changes the machine init() builds (on the Next it decides the boot-ROM overlay), and so how the recording replays. Any other snapshot type fails the load: input replayed against a machine it was not recorded on reproduces nothing.

For the same reason a playback builds the machine the recording was made on. The recorder names it in the RZX creator block's custom data (rzx::set_recorded_machine(), machine=48k — a --machine value), because the snapshot cannot always: an older Next recording embeds a 48K SNA, which names no machine. rzx::recorded_machine() reads that marker first and otherwise judges a recording by its snapshot (snapshot_machine(), the same single table the snapshot loaders use: SNA size, SZX machine ID, .z80 version and hardware mode); a pre-marker jnext recording with an SNA names no machine. emulator_boot_machine() turns that into the machine a boot builds, and every boot that plays a recording asks it: main.cpp for the command line (unless --machine was given explicitly — load_rzx() then warns on a mismatch) and emulator_cold_boot() for every cold boot, which is the GUI's route. The shared cold-boot driver hands the booted type back to the frontend (ColdBootHooks::keep_machine), so the recording's machine stays selected for later boots, a hard reset included, and MainWindow::set_emulator() shows it.

A recording cannot replay a reset the host performs, so none is ever carried across one. The power-on cold boot, the host's F4 soft reset and starting a playback all go through Emulator::end_rzx_at_reset(), which writes the running recording and ends it there, with a warning — the choice FUSE makes on a menu reset or on opening a file. (A reset the program asks for itself, through NR 0x02, replays like any other instruction and ends nothing.) jnext's reader and writer handle one snapshot and one input sequence per file, so continuing across the reset with a second snapshot block — which the RZX format allows — is not an option they offer. A file from elsewhere that does continue from a second snapshot (FUSE writes one for an inserted snapshot) is played up to it: rzx::parse() stops there and counts the rest in RzxRecording::later_snapshots, and load_rzx() warns.

docs.title: POK trainers
docs.text:
A .pok file (the World of Spectrum format: N name, M/Z pokes of bank address value original, Y end) is a list of cheats for one game. It is the one input here that is not loaded into a fresh machine: it edits the machine that is running, so it is written as a client of the debugger backend (jnext::pok, src/platform/pok_trainers.*, namespace jnext::pok) and holds no Emulator*. Every read is Debugger::peek and every write is Debugger::poke(CLIENT_NONE, MemSpace::page(p), ...), which is what gives the trainers, with no code of their own, the RZX refusal (a recording would diverge), the rewind wall (note_mutation(): Step Back across a trainer is refused, as for any debugger edit), the beam-replay logging of a page store (log_page_store()) and a MUTATE line per byte. A second write path (a direct Mmu or Ram store) would lose each of those; do not add one.

The module has no Qt, so pok_trainers_test runs in make unit-test, unit-test-sdl and unit-test-win. The Qt side is gui/pok_dialog.* (a view of a Session) and MainWindow::open_pok_file(), the seam both Machine ▸ POK Trainers… and File ▸ Load of a .pok end in; pok_dialog_test drives the real menu action, file picker, dialog and value prompt. --load x.pok keeps its "unsupported file extension" refusal: a .pok is not a program. The runs that have no window (headless, and the SDL-only window) take one through two options, --delayed-pok-frames N FILE and --pok-trainers LIST (below); a script (set mem[a], set phys[p, o], save_snapshot) still does what the options do not, and the recipe is in the user guide (5.11).

From the command line. Two rows in cli_options.h, not one, because the table's arity is at most 2 (CLI-TBL-03) and because "when, and which file" and "which trainers" are different things; main.cpp refuses either without the other, or either twice. The parse arms only store. Below the loop main() reads and checks everything that can be checked before the machine exists, so a typo in a CI script fails at once with status 1: parse_picks() turns the list (1,3=9,7: a trainer number from 1, optionally =VALUE) into Picks, make_cli_request() loads the file and checks the picks against it (the trainer exists and is valid, a value is given exactly for a trainer that leaves one open) into a CliRequest. The Qt window has the dialog, so main() refuses the options there (#ifdef ENABLE_QT_UI, not headless). configure_and_run hands the request to HeadlessApp::set_delayed_pok() or SdlApp::set_delayed_pok(); QtApp has none, and if constexpr leaves the call out of its instantiation.

Each of the two loops holds a jnext::pok::CliJob: the request and a cli::Delay::frames(N). poll() runs once per tick, after that tick's --load, --inject and --rzx-record handling and before its frame, so --load x.sna with N = 0 applies the trainers right after the snapshot is in; otherwise they go in on the poll after N frames have run. When due it calls run_cli_request(): a fresh Session over the loop owner's debugger backend (the same write path, so the same RZX refusal, rewind wall and MUTATE lines), apply() for each pick in the order written, stopping at the first refusal with the trainer's number and name in the reason; a trainer that state() already reports as found in memory is logged and left. A refusal makes poll() return false, which the loop turns into exit_code_ = 1, and a job still pending when the automatic exit fires is listed in auto_exit_finds_no_deferred_work(), so neither can end in a quiet exit 0. Nothing is removed from here: a run is one-shot. The rows are POK-60..64 (the list, the request, the run, the refusal, the job's counting) and the regression row delayed-pok-func, which reads the trainers back from a .scr (the ULA screen memory, byte for byte) in both loops, with the controls that a frame earlier or later flips, the --load order, the banked line, the usage errors and the Qt refusal.

Where a poke lands. Only 0xC000-0xFFFF is banked. Port 0x7FFD writes MMU6 and MMU7 and nothing else (zxnext.vhd:4679-4680; MMU2-5 keep pages 0A 0B 04 05, zxnext.vhd:4613-4616), so a Multiface-level POKE with a bank number can only reach that bank at 0xC000 and above. A banked poke (bank 0-7) at address ≥ 0xC000 is NR page 2*bank + ((address >> 13) & 1), offset address & 0x1FFF, whatever is paged in (a 48K only has bank 0 there: port 0x7FFD is not decoded, NR 0x82 = 0xC0). Every other poke (bank 8-15, "ignore the bank", or an address below 0xC000) is the RAM page Debugger::mmu_slots() reports for the address when the trainer is applied, not poke(Cpu), which would follow a Layer 2 write-over mapping that reads do not. Fuse and ZEsarUX index RAM[bank][address & 0x3FFF] for every address; that differs from this only for a banked line below 0xC000, a few lines in thousands of real files, all in trainers that also poke the banked window, and it is not the author's reading. On the real 128K Starglider (loaded from its tape, snapshot at the title), "Infinite Missiles (Bank#0)" is M 0 44796 2 0 / Z 0 60367 0 0. The second line lands in bank 0, on the DEC A that counts the missile counter down (it becomes a NOP). The first is the CPU address 0xAEFC (bank 2), the operand of the LD A,1 that resets the same counter; read as byte 0x2EFC of bank 0, as Fuse and ZEsarUX read it, it changes an unrelated byte of bank 0 instead and the reset stays 1 (a bank diff of two snapshots, with and without the trainer, shows exactly those two bytes). The decision, the evidence and what would reopen it are in doc/analysis/POK-BANKED-POKES-BELOW-C000.md.

Undo and state. Session::apply resolves every poke to a location, reads every original before writing anything (so a refusal leaves memory untouched and a trainer that pokes one address twice restores the byte from before the trainer), writes the last value of each location, and keeps {location, original, final} per trainer. remove writes those originals back to those locations, whatever is paged in by then. state() is derived from memory, never stored: Applied needs a record whose bytes all still hold; AppliedFound is a trainer with no value left open whose bytes are all in memory with no record (removable only if every poke gives a non-zero original). A record that stops verifying is kept, because removing an overlapping trainer can make it true again. When the program has overwritten part of a trainer it reads Not applied and Remove is refused, so Apply is the way on; it replaces the record, but a location that still holds what the older record wrote keeps the older record's original (matched by page and offset), because that byte is still our poke, and a location the program changed takes the program's byte. Without that, Remove would leave the poke in place for good. A program put in through the backend, which never reaches set_emulator(), drops them too: the Session compares Debugger::program_loads() and forgets the records when it moved (POK-65..67, once per move, for every trainer). The counter moves for a ZRCP smartload (Debugger::load(), whether the loader succeeded or not), a ZRCP load-binary that landed a byte, and a NEW DZRP or GDB session (note_program_replaced() from cmd_init and the GDB on_connect: neither protocol has a load verb, the program arrives as memory writes after the connection; DZRP-LOAD-01, GDB-SES-08, ZRCP-LOAD-06). Plain memory writes into a session already open (CMD_WRITE_MEM/BANK, M/X, write-memory) do not move it, so the records survive those. forget_applied() drops them for the other routes: MainWindow::set_emulator() calls it, and QtApp calls set_emulator() after every machine rebuild (boot_machine()'s rewire_host hook), which covers menu load, Quick Load, Power Reset, a guest NR 0x02 reset and a machine-type change.

File > Load. handle_load_path() sends a .pok to open_pok_file() before any cold boot. The same function now also refuses, before the cold boot, a file that would route to the NEX loader (a .nex, or an extension nothing owns) but has no Next prologue (NexLoader::probe_version()), which NexLoader::load() would refuse anyway: before, the session was reset and then the load failed. The reason follows the case: a .nex is "not a NEX file" and nothing more, and only an extension nothing owns is told the list of formats and where a .pok goes.

The suites: pok_trainers_test (POK-01..25 and POK-60 the parser, the list and load_pok_file, POK-30..57 and POK-61..64 the session and the command-line request, each bank-to-page row citing zxnext.vhd or the other emulators' indexing and asserting bytes the test placed itself; the rows that sweep a trainer's locations one at a time, POK-50..52, are there so that a rule meant for every location cannot pass by checking the first) and pok_dialog_test (PKD-01..17); File > Load's refusal is preferences_apply_test PA-24e/f/g.

docs.title: ZIP archives
docs.text:
game.tap.zip loads by being turned into an extracted file with the member's own extension at the two places a user names a program: the command-line fold in main.cpp (right after the bare filename becomes load_file, before the RZX checks) and MainWindow::handle_load_path(). Every decision below that, from the extension tables to the warm start, the RZX and snapshot rules, the V1.3 gate, Debugger::load_program_sidecars and the NEX loader that keeps its file open (ExtendedNexHost::reopen(), run X.nex siblings resolved beside it), then sees an ordinary path and is unchanged. Loading from memory per format was rejected: nine loader APIs, and a NEX needs a path anyway.

Two readers, on purpose. save/zip_archive.* is the .jns container: it accepts only the subset its own writer emits (flag 0, no extra field, no data descriptor, lower-case grammar paths) and must stay that strict, because two readers disagreeing about the bytes is the failure it exists to avoid. Real archives break every one of those rules (Info-ZIP: flag 0x0002, a 24-byte extra field on every entry, directory entries; streaming writers: flag 0x0008 and zero sizes in the local header), so save/zip_interchange.* is a separate read-only reader: sizes and CRC from the CENTRAL directory, the data offset from the LOCAL header's own name and extra lengths, stored and deflate only, and a refusal naming each of: not an archive, ZIP64, multi-disk, a damaged directory (archive level), encryption, another method, a declared size over 256 MiB (checked before anything is allocated), a CRC mismatch (member level). The only code the two share is zip::inflate_exact(); the EOCD and central-directory walks are not shared, because a shared walk has to be the weaker of the two. ZIPI-25 pins that the strict reader still refuses an Info-ZIP archive.

core/program_archive.* is the layer on top. is_program_ext() is the ONE table of loadable extensions and emulator_load_routes_to_nex() is defined over it, so they cannot drift. is_archive_path() is false for a program extension or .pok (a .jns IS a zip), true for any .zip, and for anything else true when the file starts PK\3\4 or PK\5\6. ProgramArchive lists the members that are programs (not directories, __MACOSX/ or ._ AppleDouble junk), refuses two with one name, and extracts to <config-dir>/archive-load/<process>/<n>/<basename> after refusing an absolute, drive-lettered or .. name (splitting on both / and \, APPNOTE 4.4.17) and sanitising the basename. Several programs are refused on the command line (listed) and asked for in the window (QInputDialog; refused with the list when unattended, and the choice mapped back by INDEX, never by re-encoding the text). Duplicate names are found with a hash set (a find() per member was quadratic: 12 s for 65534 entries). A member name is untrusted bytes: every message that carries one goes through display_name(), which escapes C0, DEL, C1 and anything outside well-formed UTF-8 as \xNN, so no consumer can print an escape sequence. An archive file over 256 MiB is refused too, before it is read. extraction_name() also prefixes _ to a Windows device name (CON.TAP, NUL.Z80, COM1.NEX), on every OS, because Windows 10 refuses to create those files.

Lifetime. One ScratchDir per process (process_scratch(), a function-local static, so it is destroyed on any return from main(), after the app objects and their open NEX handle, which matters on Windows): a random directory per process, one numbered slot per extraction (two archives both holding GAME.TAP never collide, and a refused second load never removes the file the running program has open). Process directories older than 7 days are swept on first use: leftovers of a crash, never another instance's live session. In the window, a bundled .pok (matching_pok(): same stem, else the only one) becomes the POK session without showing the dialog (start_pok_session(.., show=false)).

The suites: program_archive_test (ZIPI-01..25 the reader, ZIPL-01..22 the layer; fixtures from foreign writers in test/fixtures/zip plus archives built in code with test/zip_fixture.h), load_error_test ZIPG-01..09 (the window) and the zip-load-func regression row.

docs.title: Media out
docs.text:
What Flag / UI Code PNG or .SCR screenshot --delayed-screenshot, File ▸ Save Screenshot, File ▸ Quick Screenshot src/core/screenshot.* WAV of the mixer --wav-record src/audio/audio_recorder.* DAC activity CSV --dac-trace src/audio/dac_trace_recorder.* MP4 with audio --record, File ▸ Record MPEG4 Video src/core/video_recorder.*

Two formats, and the extension is the only selector. There is no format flag and no format argument anywhere: screenshot_format_for_path() reads the filename's last extension, and save_screenshot() is the single dispatch every caller goes through — the three frontends' --delayed-screenshot handlers and both GUI menu entries. Adding a third format means adding it there, once.

PNG screenshots are always written at double height — each framebuffer row is emitted twice — so that a 640×256 frame becomes a 640×512 PNG with square pixels and the aspect ratio a viewer expects. --delayed-screenshot-layers narrows a capture by clearing layer enables in the renderer rather than by masking the result, so the layers that remain still follow NR 0x15 priority; see 3.3 Video.

.SCR is not a rendering at all. Ula::screen_dump() copies the ULA's own storage through fetch_vram_bank() — the same function the pixel and attribute fetches use — so the file is the bytes the display is reading, not a conversion of the composited picture. Bank and layout come from the live register state exactly as the renderer derives them: the port 0x7FFD shadow bit alone chooses bank 5 or bank 7 (zxnext.vhd:6649-6656), and port 0xFF bits 2:0 choose the window, masked back to the standard mode while shadow is on (zxula.vhd:191). Standard and Timex-alt give 6912 bytes; hi-colour and hi-res give 12288, the two 6144-byte planes the ULA fetches. Nothing else in the machine is representable, so a Layer 2 or tilemap program captured this way yields whatever is left in the ULA screen memory — a documented limitation of the format, not of the dump.

--delayed-screenshot-layers is refused with a .scr target rather than ignored (src/main.cpp), for the same reason it is refused without a screenshot at all: an option that silently does nothing is worse than an error.

Both writers treat a failed fclose() as a failure. That is not defensive noise: a screenshot is small enough to sit entirely in stdio's buffer, so on a full disk the only write(2) happens at the close, and ignoring its result is precisely how a truncated file gets reported as saved.

Quick Screenshot (File ▸ Quick Screenshot, Alt+K) is the same write with no dialog: auto_screenshot_path() builds jnext-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS<ext> in the configured directory, creating it if needed and appending -02, -03… while the name is taken. Its directory and format are separate config fields from the Save-Screenshot dialog's remembered directory, deliberately — that one follows the dialog around, and a no-dialog capture whose destination moves is unfindable.

Quick Save / Quick Load (File ▸ Quick Save Snapshot Alt+Shift+F5, Quick Load Snapshot Alt+Shift+F9; the same two chords in the SDL-only build) follow the same shape for .jns. src/core/quick_snapshot.* holds the folder (default_quick_snapshot_dir() = sdcard::default_state_dir() + /snapshots, so $JNEXT_CONFIG_DIR and the SD image's own state-dir resolution apply — on Windows, with no HOME, it is under %USERPROFILE%\.jnext: home_dir() tries HOME, then USERPROFILE, else .), the name (auto_timestamped_path(), the one function auto_screenshot_path() also uses) and the choice of file (latest_quick_snapshot(): greatest modification time among *.jns regular files directly in the folder, ties to the greater name stem so …-02 beats the bare name; local-time names are not ordered across a DST change, which is why the name is not the key). Quick Load goes through MainWindow::handle_load_path() / SdlApp::cold_boot(), i.e. a full cold boot and then load_jns_file(), never an in-place load. Two things make that route safe for a .jns: Emulator::probe_jns_file() runs the pre-touch half of load_jns (check_jns()) BEFORE the cold boot, so a file that will be refused costs no session; and emulator_boot_machine() reads the .jns manifest's machine the way it reads an RZX's, so the cold boot builds the snapshot's machine and the frontend's keep_machine hook records it (otherwise a later reset would boot the old machine); the command-line startup does the same through emulator_startup_machine(), where a .jns wins even over an explicit --machine. After ANY snapshot load the frontends' emulator_apply_load() calls Keyboard::release_all_keys(): the membrane matrix in a .jns records the keys the host held at save time (the Shift of the Alt+Shift+F5 chord), whose release would never arrive, so the guest starts with no key down (the matrix, the extended-key register that the arrows use, and the shift scan history; the core load keeps them, the round-trip contract: QS-28..30). Debugger-initiated loads (DZRP, ZRCP, GDB) go through emulator_apply_load() too, so they release held keys as well. prune_quick_snapshots() never deletes a symbolic link. Quick Load failures (no snapshot, unreadable newest file) are a status-bar line in Qt and a log line in SDL, never a dialog; both actions act once per key press (QuickChordTracker, setAutoRepeat(false)). .sna, .szx and .z80 switch machine the same way (see "Which machine a snapshot loads as" below), and QS-25..27 pin that route. Retention: prune_quick_snapshots() runs after each Quick Save and deletes only names matching is_quick_snapshot_name(); the count is EmulatorConfig::quick_snapshot_keep (CLI) or AppConfigData::quick_snapshot_keep ([snapshot] quick_keep, Preferences), the CLI winning (quick_snapshot_keep_cli). The debugger keymap refuses Alt+Shift+F5/F9 by name (validate_combo). The SDL chord predicate is platform/quick_snapshot_chord.h; the Qt chords are the two QAction shortcuts in main_window.cpp. Both frontends hand the request to the key Router (on_host_action()) instead of acting in the key callback, so a chord takes its turn behind the keys typed before it, keys typed during or after it reach the loaded machine, and SdlApp::service_quick_requests() / QtApp::TickEffects::post_frames() call action_done() however the action ended (see the input subsystem chapter). There is no whole-card read on this path (owner decision, 2026-10-22): a save, probe or load reads the MBR and the BPB sector (the Tier-1 identity) and nothing else; .jns has no Tier-2 content_stamp any more (old files carry one, it is ignored) and no mid-transfer refusal. jnext assumes the card is as the snapshot left it. sd_no_digest_linux_test (NODIG-01..04) pins it by bytes read.

Video recording needs FFmpeg on the host. jnext writes raw ARGB frames and raw stereo PCM to temporary files during the run, so the hot loop pays no encoding cost, and shells out once at stop, trying libx264, mpeg4 and libopenh264 in that order. The command line is built for two dialects — POSIX sh and Windows CreateProcess — and both are compiled everywhere, so both stay unit-testable on any host.

docs.title: The SD card is two independent things
docs.text:
jnext talks to the same .img file in two entirely different ways, at two different times, for two different consumers. The split looks redundant until you notice that the two consumers want opposite things.

src/core/sd_rom_extractor.* is a host-side FAT32 reader. Before the machine can start, jnext needs the ROM images that on real hardware live as files on the card, and there is no guest yet to ask for them — so the emulator opens the .img as a filesystem and pulls them out by path: /MACHINES/NEXT/48.rom, 128.rom, plus3.rom, enNxtmmc.rom, enNextMf.rom and enAltZX.rom. It is read-only, handles MBR + FAT32-LBA only, and does short-name lookup only, which is all that job needs.

src/peripheral/sd_card.cpp is emulated hardware. Once the machine is running, the guest wants a card, not a filesystem: NextZXOS carries its own FAT driver and expects to do the filesystem work itself, over SPI, one 512-byte block at a time. That class implements an SD card in SPI mode behind the SpiDevice interface and serves those blocks over ports 0xE7/0xEB — see 3.6 Peripherals. It knows nothing about FAT32.

The two never talk to each other: one serves the host at init time, the other the guest at run time. The card is opened read-write and guest writes persist, so booting the machine mutates the image; --sdcard-readonly makes the guest see a write-protected card instead.

Provisioning is a third, separate concern. sdcard_provisioner.* locates or downloads the canonical image and re-clusters a copy via fat32_image.*, because the shipped 1 GB image has too few clusters to be a spec-valid FAT32 and the Next firmware's own FatFs — correctly — rejects it. The same pass writes a default /MACHINES/NEXT/config.ini and doubles the distribution's 16 KB zx81.rom to the 32 KB the firmware boot menu loads (as upstream tbblue did after the 24.11 release), only when it is that exact file. That recipe is versioned (kFixedImageRecipe, recorded in a .recipe sidecar next to the image). jnext never rebuilds an existing image because its recipe is old: the image holds the user's own files.

Downloads are resumable, by one contract for every caller of DownloadFn (the SD distro zip, the NextPi archive, its .md5, the mirror listing). The default backends (libcurl, WinHTTP) write <dest>.part, beside a resume record <dest>.part.resume (requested URL, validator, full size), and rename it over dest only when the byte count matches the advertised total, so dest exists only when complete and a transfer cut short is a failure on both OSes. A failure or cancel keeps the partial only if it holds bytes and the server sent a strong ETag (else Last-Modified); otherwise nothing is left. The next call asks for the rest (Range, If-Range with the validator verbatim) and decides before the first body byte: 206 with exactly the expected Content-Range appends; 200 (range ignored or representation changed) starts again from 0; 416 or a wrong 206 discards the partial and retries once as a plain GET. libcurl uses CURLOPT_RANGE with an explicit If-Range header, not CURLOPT_RESUME_FROM_LARGE, which turns a server's 200 into error 33 and loses the transfer. The file names, the record format and the decision table live once in PartialDownload (sdcard_provisioner.cpp); both backends only feed it headers and body. Residual corruption (a server that lies about its validator) is caught after the download: the NextPi MD5, the zip entry CRC. One classifier (partial_state) names the five states of a .part: a Complete one (whole file, only the final rename failed) is finished with no request and never refetched; an Oversize or Stale one is discarded; a Resumable one is continued, appended at an explicit 64-bit offset.

A dropped network must neither freeze the window nor take minutes to be noticed. The same contract on DownloadFn says how both backends behave while a transfer is under way. They call the ProgressFn at least every tick_ms (200), whatever the network does: connecting, waiting for headers, a silent body. A false from it ends the attempt within a tick (cancelled by user, the partial kept by the rule above). An attempt that gets no body byte for stall_timeout_ms (30 000, counted from the start of the attempt and then from the last byte) ends with stalled: no data received for 30 s (after X of Y bytes), the partial kept the same way, and a slow transfer that is alive is never cut. The download runs on the GUI thread, before QtApp exists, so the window lives exactly as often as a backend calls SdcardGuiProvisioner::progress, which pumps the event loop: the cadence is the backends' business, not a worker thread's. The rule exists once. StallWatch answers "how long since the byte count last changed", download_step is the per-tick decision both backends take (report, honour a cancel, test the watch), DownloadTimings carries the two numbers and the WinHTTP read size (tests pass short ones to http_download; default_http_download forwards the production values), and the dialog uses the same watch for its notice: once 5 s (kStallNoticeMs) pass with no byte its label gains Stalled: no data received for N s, the seconds counting up and the note gone when bytes arrive. The dialog's watch starts when it opens, so a slow answer to the confirm box is not a stall.

The libcurl twin runs the transfer on the multi interface: curl_multi_perform, download_step, then curl_multi_poll for one tick. With the easy interface the progress callback is frequent while data flows but slows to about one call a second when nothing arrives (libcurl documents it; 1.00 s gaps measured through a 15 s stall), so the window repainted at about 1 Hz through a stall and nothing named the stall; CURLOPT_LOW_SPEED_* is gone because its moving average overshot (120 s set, 126 s measured) and a second mechanism would be a second message. curl_multi_poll needs libcurl 7.66, which every packaged target exceeds. A file:// URL (a test seam, and the Flatpak build) is read inside one curl_multi_perform call and has no ticks. The WinHTTP twin is asynchronous (WINHTTP_FLAG_ASYNC) because the contract cannot be met synchronously: a synchronous WinHttpReadData blocks its thread until data arrives or its receive timeout fires, and Microsoft documents closing a synchronous request's handle from another thread as a race. With the cable pulled the GUI thread sat inside that read for its 120 s, and Windows ghosted the window as "Not Responding". In async mode the thread waits on a condition variable (with an SRW lock) for the next completion or the next tick by the clock, and a cancel or a stall is "close the request handle and return". The wait is not a kernel event on purpose: under wine without ntsync every kernel-object wait goes through the single-threaded wineserver, which also delivers its timeout, so a wineserver that does not run for T seconds delays the tick by T (a 1 s stop gave a 1.2 s tick gap, the CI failure of PROV-STALL-08). A condition-variable wait is a futex inside the process under wine and a kernel wait on Windows (Vista and later, so Windows 7 is covered). That holds only while no WinHTTP call made on that thread waits on the network. WinHttpReceiveResponse may: wine 11.7 and later read the headers inside the call, in its caller (no tick, no stall note and no cancel for the whole header wait, up to 21 s, until the server closed). Microsoft's sentence that even in async mode a function "can operate either synchronously or asynchronously" is on WinHttpSendRequest and WinHttpQueryDataAvailable too, and the waiting thread still calls those and WinHttpReadData. What makes them safe is wine's source and measurement, not the documentation: SendRequest is always queued (wine 11.0 and 11.20), and QueryDataAvailable and ReadData complete in the caller only with data already buffered (the reads ask for no more than was reported available). So the sequence is "send; the receive is started from the SENDREQUEST_COMPLETE callback, Microsoft's reentrant pattern; the waiting thread no longer waits for the server's answer inside a WinHTTP call". Established: wine 11.0 and 11.20, by source and by the rows; Windows only by inference from the documentation. The remaining gap: a SendRequest that completed synchronously and delivered SENDREQUEST_COMPLETE on the calling thread would run the receive on the waiting thread again; impossible under wine, unknown on Windows. The callback returns without signalling after a successful call (HEADERS_AVAILABLE or REQUEST_ERROR may be delivered nested inside it and set the state themselves), and the waiting thread treats HEADERS_AVAILABLE as done only once that call has returned (Microsoft: wait for the function to return and the completion callback before another operation on the handle). Closing the handle while the callback thread is inside the call is what the concurrency rules forbid, so a handoff under the state's SRW lock decides who closes: a waiting thread that gives up while the receive is in flight marks the request abandoned and the callback closes it when the call returns, otherwise the waiting thread closes it itself; either way once, and the callback touches nothing after its own close. The per-request state (lock and condition variable, latest completion, read buffer, the extra headers WinHttpSendRequest still points at) is heap-allocated and belongs to the request handle from the moment the status callback is installed: the callback frees it on WINHTTP_CALLBACK_STATUS_HANDLE_CLOSING, the last callback a handle gets, so an abort returns at once while WinHTTP may still be completing a read into that buffer, and nothing touches the state after WinHttpCloseHandle. The callback stores atomics, signals and starts the receive (no logging, no globals) and is declared CALLBACK, which the i686 builds need. Reads are sized by WinHttpQueryDataAvailable, so every byte that arrived reaches the .part, and a read never asks for more than the buffer holds (DownloadTimings::read_bytes, 64 KiB); the receive timeout is only a backstop 30 s behind the stall timeout.

Under wine the rows (PROV-STALL-*, PIT-43) show the tick cadence, the stall, the cancel and the resume on the WinHTTP backend; they cannot show five things. Windows' own hung-window detection (five seconds without a message pump) and the Qt dialog on top of WinHTTP: the Qt suites run on Linux only, so the pump is proven there (SDD-01..03) and meets the WinHTTP cadence in progress(), which every platform shares. A physical cable pull (media sense, TCP retransmission, RST or ICMP): the loopback server models "connection open, nothing arrives", which is what a receiver sees until TCP gives up. WinHTTP's teardown of a pending asynchronous read: wine keeps it until data, EOF, the server's close or the backstop (measured 58 s), so a row that abandons a connection builds its own server and lets its destructor close it; the caller's result and timing are the same, only the abandoned socket lives longer (under wine 11.7 and later this includes the header wait of an abandoned attempt: it holds wine's queue thread until the server closes or 21 s pass). The close handoff itself is not observable: wine keeps a request object alive while a call holds it, so closing mid-call is tolerated and removing the handoff passes every row; it rests on Microsoft's rule and on review, and PROV-STALL-11 pins the user-visible half (cancel before the server has answered). The tick's independence from the wineserver: it is measured by stopping the wineserver for a second during PROV-STALL-08, not by a row, because a stalled wineserver stalls every suite sharing the prefix. And TLS under asynchronous WinHTTP, and the read-fill semantics and error codes of real Windows (wine fills the buffer, reports a read timeout as 10060 and never reports more than 8 KiB available: measured over the whole provisioner suite, 8192 at most): the rows use plain http on loopback, and https to the real mirrors is exercised only by use. How much real Windows reports available is therefore not observable here; the clamp of a read to the buffer binds under wine only because PROV-STALL-10 lowers read_bytes to 1000, and the buffer is the one limit that does not depend on that number. The error side is pinned the same way: PROV-STALL-09 makes a server close without answering and a port refuse the connection, one per stage of the asynchronous sequence, and requires the transport's own reason at once, never a stall.

What a failed fetch says is the callers' business, once. Every failure of a fetch is built by sdcard::fetch_failure(what, url, reason, next): <what>: <reason>, then URL: <url> (exactly the string handed to the DownloadFn, one variable per fetch, so it can be pasted into a browser), then <what happens next> (the part is kept, nothing was kept, the download was removed); nine call sites, two in sdcard_provisioner.cpp and seven in nextpi_provisioner.cpp, and nothing else builds one. The backends hand up a reason in plain words and no framing: net_reason(kind, raw) gives each NetFailure kind its one wording and appends the backend's own code and text in parentheses, http_status_reason(status) does the same for an HTTP error status (RFC 9110 section 15), and each twin defines transport_reason(code) (like http_download), which sorts its codes into the kinds: a CURLcode for libcurl, an ERROR_WINHTTP_* for WinHTTP, wine's WSAETIMEDOUT as a timeout. So the two say the same words for the same failure. libcurl's CURLOPT_FAILONERROR turns any HTTP status of 400 or more into one generic code, so that twin reads the status off the transfer, and a 404 reads the same as on WinHTTP (where PartialDownload::begin says it, through the same function). A proxy that will not open the tunnel (its answer to CONNECT is not a 2xx) leaves the transfer with no response status at all, so that twin also reads CURLINFO_HTTP_CONNECTCODE and says could not connect to the server (the proxy answered HTTP 403 to the connection request), whatever code libcurl gave the failure (8.18: 22 for a 4xx or 5xx, 56 for a 3xx). WinHTTP takes its proxy from the machine's settings, never from the environment, so the case exists only on libcurl. libcurl also gives its codes 1 and 3 (unsupported protocol, malformed URL) to a reply it cannot use after connecting (not HTTP, or a redirect to a scheme or URL it cannot follow); only with no connection made (CURLINFO_NUM_CONNECTS 0) is that the address's fault, so only then is it worded as one. The stall reason, cancelled by user and the other reasons that were already plain are unchanged, as are the declared residuals (curl_easy_init failed, which the user cannot act on). PROV-REASON-01..05 pin the wordings, 04 on both transports (it fails on both with the old text) and 05 the transport's own code for an address it cannot use; PROV-REASON-06 and 07 put a refusing proxy, and a server whose reply libcurl cannot use, in front of the real libcurl backend, which is why they live in the POSIX-only sibling suite sdcard_provisioner_posix_test; PROV-MSG-* and PIT-44..50 the messages, PROV-SANDBOX-02 and PROV-STALL-09 moved to the new text with their invariants intact.

Where the message goes. main.cpp logs a failed SD-card provisioning in every frontend (headless and the SDL-only build printed it to stderr and nowhere else) and shows it in a dialog in the Qt GUI; a failed NextPi start is reported in a dialog in the Qt GUI whether it came from Preferences (jnext starts without it) or from --nextpi (it also prints to stderr and exits 1); and the warning that latest could not read the mirror's list is a dialog too, not only a log line. A declined release change is the user's own answer and is logged, not a warning. SdcardGuiProvisioner::warn shows a QMessageBox built by warning_box, whose text is selectable by mouse whatever the widget style (the "Windows" style's default is links only, so the address could not be copied). On the offscreen platform nothing is shown (nobody could dismiss it); the title and the text go to the platform logger at debug level, and that line is what sdcard-download-fail-func and nextpi-func facts 10-12 read of a dialog.

The short fetches. The NextPi release list of latest and the two .md5 fetches are tiny, so they passed no ProgressFn, and on a dead network the window showed nothing for the 30 s the backend waits. ShortFetchFn (nextpi::ProvisionOptions:: short_fetch) wraps exactly those three, with a label and the address each, and hands the fetch the ProgressFn it should give the DownloadFn; the archive download is not wrapped and keeps opts.progress (PIT-51). The Qt build's SdcardGuiProvisioner::short_fetch pumps the event loop on every call, shows nothing for the first kShortFetchShowMs (1000 ms, so a quick fetch does not flash a dialog), and then shows the same dialog as the archive, built and refreshed by the same code (title, empty bar, Stalled notice from 5 s, Cancel); it is gone when the fetch returns. Its Cancel ends that fetch only: the cancelled_ latch of progress() is not touched, so the archive download that follows is not aborted. All of it counts on the helper's now_(), so SDD-06..08 run on a clock the test owns, and SDD-09 runs the whole thing through the real backend and a silent server on the production clock. nextpi-func fact 12 shows it in the real binary against a mirror that answers after 3 s.

The console. The frontends with no dialog (--headless, the SDL-only build) say the same things as text, on stderr and in the log, in the dialog's words. One class decides: sdcard::ConsoleWait is made for one transfer and ticked by its ProgressFn, which the backends call at least every 200 ms whatever the network does. When no byte has arrived for kStallNoticeMs (5 s) it says stall_note(), the dialog's own text, once, on a line of its own on stderr and as a warning in the log, and again if bytes come and a new stall begins. With a slow_line it also says that line once, as information, when the transfer has gone on for kShortFetchShowMs; a quicker transfer says nothing at all. The limit is the dialog's, defined once in the core. A ConsoleWait counts from its first tick, not from its construction: the prompt before a download can sit open for minutes. nextpi::CliShortFetch is the console's ShortFetchFn: one ConsoleWait per fetch, its line <label> <address>, logged on the uart logger like the rest of the module. sdcard::CliProgress is the terminal's progress display of a download, the \rDownloading ... 45% line that cli_progress and the NextPi twin drew, now one class with the heading and the no-length rule as arguments (the SD-card image counts MiB, NextPi says nothing) and the stall note, which starts a new line when a progress line was left unfinished. make_cli_progress() makes the SD-card image's and nextpi::make_cli_progress() NextPi's; main.cpp wires them, and CliShortFetch, where there is no dialog. The clock, the stream and the log's copy are parameters, so PROV-CON-01..11 and PIT-52..56 run all of it on a fake clock and read the stream back as a file; the real binary is shown by sdcard-download-fail-func fact 5 (both frontends without a dialog, each with its own wiring in main.cpp) and nextpi-func fact 13, against a server that answers after 8 s. What no row can show is the NextPi archive's own display being wired in main.cpp: its download needs 22 GB free, which the regression suite cannot assume, so that one assignment is covered only by the classes it uses.

docs.title: 3.9.1 The backend API
docs.text:
Four headers in src/debug/ are the whole interface a frontend sees:

Header Declares debugger.h jnext::dbg::Debugger, and the session types: ClientKind, ClientInfo, Listener, Service, PumpBudget, ServiceHint, PausedInfo, StopPolicy, LoopDriver, LogLevel events.h the event vocabulary: EventKind and its sub-kinds, Event, EventFilter, Subscription, SubscriptionInfo, Condition, Handler, Action, Hit, ClientId, EventId inspect.h the inspection value types: MemSpace, SlotInfo, RegId, RunState, PauseReason, Time, MachineInfo, RewindRange, InputState, Layer, ClipLayer, PaletteId and the rest result.h Result, the closed set of refusals, and Expected<T>

They are a frozen interface. A verb is added only by owner decision, and each declaration says which capability id of doc/design/DEBUG-SUBSYSTEM-ARCHITECTURE.md §4 it serves. doc/design/debug-subsystem/b0-cap-traceability.md maps each capability id to its declarations, though not completely: rgb333_to_argb(), for one, is missing from it.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
Every verb that can refuse returns a Result. The set is closed, and every value is pinned by debug_types_check.cpp:

Value Result Meaning 0 Ok done 1 RefusedRunning needs a paused machine 2 RefusedPaused needs a running machine 3 RefusedCorrupt an unacknowledged corruption incident blocks it (CTL-11) 4 RefusedRzx an RZX is recording or playing 5 RefusedUnavailable benign: the thing is not there right now (empty rewind buffer, trace off, no loop driver, an unknown bookmark) 6 RefusedReadOnly a ROM target 7 InvalidPage a page number that names no page 8 NotAtFrameBoundary a frame-boundary-only verb, mid-frame, asked not to advance 9 NoFrame a deferred capture that never got its frame 10 Unsupported there is no such thing, for example a verb called from inside an event delivery that may not be

result_name() gives each one stable lowercase spelling for logs and protocol error strings, and ok(r) is the named test for success.

A verb that refuses and also yields data returns Expected<T>: a status and a value in one object, testable with if (auto r = ...). On a refusal the value is value-initialised, with one exception: peek and poke report how many bytes did transfer even when they refuse.

A query that cannot refuse returns its value directly. The class is listed in full in debugger.h's "DIRECT-VALUE QUERIES" banner, with per-group counts so the list can be audited. Moving a query onto that list is a claim that it cannot fail. pump() is in neither class: it is the loop owner's service call.

Every transition and every mutation is attributed. A verb that pauses, resumes, steps, resets, loads or writes takes ClientId by as its first argument, and the backend broadcasts transitions with it. Reads take none. The backend itself acts as CLIENT_NONE.

No ownership token, no arbitration. One machine, any number of clients, and the last verb wins. The only thing owned is a subscription, which only the client that created it may change or remove.

Memory is addressed by MemSpace, and the index is part of the space.

MemSpace Addresses MemSpace::cpu() the live 64 KB CPU map, every overlay included (DivMMC, Multiface, Layer 2, the NR 0x8C alternate ROM) MemSpace::page(p) the physical 8 KB page p, numbered as NR 0x50-0x57 numbers it (0..223), regardless of any overlay. 0xFE and 0xFF, the ROM sentinels, answer InvalidPage MemSpace::rom(i) the 16 KB ROM image i (0..3), read-only

MemSpace is also the answer to what supplied this byte: the read arbiter (Mmu::route()) names its source with the same type, so it carries nine more kinds that only the arbiter produces: boot_rom(), multiface_rom(), multiface_ram(), divmmc_rom(), divmmc_ram(bank), alt_rom(i), layer2(page), config(bank) and floating() (nothing answers). peek and poke of one of them answer Unsupported and write nothing, until a consumer adds the access with its own rows. The type lives in debug/mem_space.h (standard headers only, so the core's memory/mmu.h can return it), and FetchSource is its name in the role of an opcode fetch's source.

A client never composes a space from a slot's page number. On the Next a ROM slot's effective_page is an un-shifted SRAM page index, outside page()'s numbering. So mmu_slots() returns each slot's complete backing store as SlotInfo::space plus SlotInfo::space_offset. rom_select() names the image legacy paging selects, even while RAM is paged at 0x0000.

space is the slot's OWN source. SlotInfo::now is what a read of the slot reaches right now, overlays included (DivMMC, Multiface, Layer 2, alt ROM, config mode, boot ROM): Mmu::route(slot << 13).space, the live data route of the slot's first byte. One value per slot is complete, because every arm of the VHDL arbiter switches on cpu_a(15:13) boundaries or coarser. It is the DATA view: the instruction at the PC may come from elsewhere, which is what source_page(pc) answers.

The spelling of a space for a human or a file (the tags P0E, ROM1, DIVRAM3..., the physical text and the AddressStyle) is debug/long_address.h. The tags are a stable format; they are described in 7.1, with the slot that holds a page >= 0xE0 and reads nothing.

docs.title: The capability families
docs.text: Each family keeps its design id prefix, which is how the headers, the tests and the design documents refer to it.

docs.title: Control — CAP-CTL
docs.text:
Verb What it does pause(by) stop at the next instruction boundary. Idempotent; a second pause re-attributes the stop to its caller run(by) resume. Still Ok on a running machine. Subject to the corruption gate step_into(by) one instruction, synchronously, frame-loop aware: a step at a HALT runs the halt out step_over(by), step_out(by) asynchronous: the stop arrives later as a Paused push run_to(by, addr), run_to_source_line(by, "file:line"), run_to_cycle(by, c), run_to_frame(by, f), run_to_end_of_frame(by), run_to_end_of_scanline(by) resume until a target. run_to_source_line arms a transient Execute group at every start of the line (each tied to its memory, subscribe_source_line); the first one reached stops the machine and the stop reads RunTo with that address. It is refused, the machine untouched, for a line with no code. A run-to issued while the machine RUNS first drops the caller's own transient targets (a second Run to Here replaces the first), never another client's step_back(by, n), rewind_to_frame(by, f) rewind, synchronously. A benign refusal is RefusedRzx or RefusedUnavailable (no ring or an empty one, a frame outside it or not recorded, the trace off or empty, or a step back that would replay across a debugger change), and logs its reason resume_blocked_by_corruption(), acknowledge_corruption(gen) the CTL-11 gate after a failed restore reset(by, Soft \| Hard) Soft is Emulator::soft_reset(). Hard is the reconstruct contract of 3.9.3 load(by, path) through the loop owner's LoopDriver::load; same contract when the load rebuilds the machine state() RunState: paused, step mode, pause_reason, cycle, frame, PC magic_breakpoint(), set_magic_breakpoint(on) the magic opcode switch armed(), persistent_breakpoints(), set_persistent_breakpoints(on) whether the hot loop consults the backend at all

step_over() asks is_call_like() about the instruction at PC (CALL, CALL cc, RST, DJNZ). If it is, it arms a transient Execute subscription at the next instruction and resumes. Otherwise it is a step_into().

docs.title: Inspection and mutation — CAP-INS
docs.text:
Reads never perturb the machine. Writes are first-class, logged by the backend, and follow the contract of 3.9.2.

Area Reads Writes registers registers() set_register(by, RegId, v), one register at a time. Setting PC clears halted memory peek(space, addr, n, buf), memory_reader() poke(by, space, addr, n, buf) paging mmu_slots(), paging_ports(), rom_select() set_mmu_slot(by, slot, page), through the NR 0x50+slot write handler NextREG nextreg_peek(reg), nextreg_selected() nextreg_write(by, reg, v), which runs the register's own handler ports — port_in(by, port), port_out(by, port, v); both dispatch like the guest's IN/OUT and are perturbing by nature time and raster time(), raster(), machine() — sprites sprites(), sprite_attr_raw(i), pattern_ram(), sprite_palette_rgb333(bank, i), sprite_clip() set_sprite_attr_raw(...), write_pattern_ram(...) Copper copper() — audio ay_registers(chip), turbosound_enabled(), ay_mode(), stereo_mode(), audio_mute_mask() set_audio_mute_mask(by, m) (host-side, never in a snapshot or an RZX) video framebuffer(), render_layer(layer, vc, dst, stride), palette(id), active_ula_palette_bank(), ula_screen_regs(), clip_window(layer) set_palette(...), set_border(by, colour) disassembly disassemble(addr, n, symbols), instruction_length(addr), is_call_like(addr) — call stack and trace call_stack(), trace_entries(), trace_export(path) set_call_stack_enabled(by, on) (a per-client request, 7.10); C variables: c_frames(), c_locals(frame), c_globals(), read_c_value(frame, path), c_variables_status() (all const, none bumps the revision), set_trace_enabled, trace_clear, trace_resize coverage coverage(), coverage_enabled(); INS-21: mem_coverage_enabled(), mem_coverage(space, addr, n, out), mem_coverage_fetch(addr), mem_coverage_spaces(), executed_source_lines(file) coverage_enable, coverage_clear; INS-21: mem_coverage_enable, mem_coverage_clear input input_state() see input injection below the event model subscriptions(include_transient), events_fired_since(seq) see 3.9.2

Three of these are worth understanding before using them.

peek(MemSpace::cpu()) is Mmu::peek(). Mmu::read() is the guest's read: it captures the byte into the +3 floating-bus latch on a contended access and raises the data-breakpoint latch on a READ watchpoint. Mmu::peek() wraps read() under DebugState::InspectionScope and puts the floating-bus byte back. It wraps rather than copies, so the overlay arbitration (boot ROM, Multiface, DivMMC, Layer 2, alternate ROM, config mode) cannot drift between the two. The trace's word at SP reads the same way.

The frame number is a tag, not the raw counter. Emulator::frame_num() is post-incremented at the start of each frame, so during frame K it reads K+1. time().frame and state().frame report frame_num() - 1. That is the tag the rewind slot for the frame carries, and the frame --delayed-keypress-frames N lands on. A rewind lands on a frame start the ring has already counted; RewindRange::at_restored_frame_start says when the machine sits on one, and run_to_frame() takes its base from it.

raster() and time() of a paused machine are snapshots taken at the query. While the machine runs they report the live beam from the clock.

render_layer() (src/debug/debugger_render.cpp) draws one of the eight Layer views of the paused frame: composite, ULA primary and shadow, Layer 2 active and shadow, sprites, tilemap, and the NR 0x4A background. It fills rows 0..vc of a RENDER_WIDTH-wide buffer with 0x00000000, so alpha 0 means transparent. It then replays every per-scanline change log the way Renderer::render_frame does, so a raster split shows as on screen. The render is state-preserving: the replay walks each log to its end, and the port 0x303B sprite status bits are saved and restored. debugger_backend_test INS-14-08 compares the whole serialised machine state around each view.

docs.title: Events — CAP-EVT
docs.text:
Verb What it does subscribe(by, Subscription) register a subscription owned by by; returns its EventId unsubscribe(by, id), set_enabled(by, id, on) owner only subscribe_source_line(by, "file:line", like) a source breakpoint: resolves the line in the live source map and subscribes one Execute per start, each a copy of like with lo = hi = start.address and space = start.space, all under one new GroupId. All or nothing; refused with no map, no code at the line, or a like that is not Execute unsubscribe_group(by, group), set_group_enabled(by, group, on) every member of a source breakpoint; owner only. SubscriptionInfo::group says which group a listed subscription belongs to (GROUP_NONE for a plain one) master_enabled(), set_master_enabled(on) suspend every non-transient subscription without touching its own flag client_enabled(cid), set_client_enabled(cid, on) the per-client switch probe_execute(pc) the ids of every live Execute subscription that would fire at pc, with its condition evaluated. A pure query, for step loops raise_host_event(by, name) raise a Host event, script1..script8 or any name up to MAX_HOST_EVENT_NAME

3.9.2 describes the subscription model and the delivery contract.

docs.title: Input injection and capture — CAP-IN, CAP-CAP
docs.text:
Pulses append. press_key(by, name | MatrixKey, hold_frames) queues a pulse on Keyboard's auto-type queue. Keyboard::queue_auto_type() appends for every producer: the phantom typist, the tape LOAD "" sites, --delayed-keypress and the backend. An append behind an entry in flight leaves that entry's counters alone, so a held key does not restart its hold. Keyboard::MAX_AUTO_TYPE_KEYS (16) caps the union of what every producer queued. A pulse that does not fit is refused with RefusedUnavailable and the count that was queued.

Every injection lands at the frame edge. A pulse or a level set (set_key, set_extended_key) issued during frame N — from a handler, from a remote command in a pump, from a CLI countdown — is applied at the end of frame N and is visible to the guest from frame N+1. The level sets are queued on Keyboard and applied first thing in the edge's tick_auto_type(), so a handler cannot change what the rest of its own frame reads. end_of_frame() delivers the Frame event before that tick, so an on frame N handler's pulse is pressed by frame N's own tick. set_joystick and press_nmi are immediate.

Screenshots wait for the next rendered frame. screenshot(by, path, layer_mask, format) only queues. pump() writes every capture whose frame has been rendered since it was queued (Emulator::rendered_frames() moved), before any command of that pump can change the machine. While a capture waits, its layer mask is armed on the renderer and a force-render bit makes sure the next frame is rendered whatever the frontend's render-skip hint says. A paused machine renders nothing, so the capture is held, with one warning. flush_captures(by) is the exit bound. It answers NoFrame if any of by's captures is still pending (they are dropped), RefusedUnavailable if one failed to write since the last call, and Ok otherwise. A capture survives its requester's detach and every machine rebuild. The PNG and .SCR writers live in src/core/screenshot.*, below the platform layer.

ula_screen_dump() returns the ULA screen as a .SCR image. Layer 2, tilemap and pattern RAM come out of peek(MemSpace::page(...)).

docs.title: State and rewind — CAP-ST
docs.text:
Saves share one rule. save_state_bytes, bookmark_save and save_snapshot reach a frame boundary through one helper. At a boundary they save. Mid-frame, SaveStateMode::RefuseMidFrame answers NotAtFrameBoundary, and AdvanceToBoundary runs the frame out under SuspendScope and logs a MUTATE clock … by <client> line, because emulated time moved under every other client. save_snapshot always advances, as --delayed-snapshot does, and writes the file by extension through save_snapshot_file() in src/core/.

A window inside the frame edge is not a boundary. Between the Frame delivery and the end of tick_auto_type() the machine is not the state run_frame() hands back, so a save from a Frame handler is refused, or answers NotAtFrameBoundary.

Bookmarks are named, in memory and per client: bookmark_save, bookmark_restore, bookmarks(cid). A client holds at most 8; a ninth new name is refused and re-saving a name replaces it. They are freed at detach and survive a hard reconstruct. A restore into a machine of another type or snapshot width is refused before load_state runs, so nothing is latched. DZRP's READ_STATE/WRITE_STATE and ZRCP's snapshot-save/snapshot-load are bookmarks.

load_state_bytes restores in-process bytes. A failure latches corruption, which the CTL-11 gate then holds every resume on. The rewind controls are rewind_enabled, set_rewind_enabled, rewind_range(), resize_rewind_buffer and rewind_blocked(), which returns the Result a rewind would refuse with, for greying a control before it is clicked. It knows only the refusals that do not depend on the target: an RZX, no ring, an empty ring. The rest — no trace entry, a frame outside the ring or not recorded, a replay that would cross a debugger change (3.9.2) — are known only when the verb runs.

A refused rewind says why. On every RefusedRzx or RefusedUnavailable, step_back and rewind_to_frame log one Warn line to every listener:

REWIND REFUSED: Step Back refused: the instruction trace is off - turn on Debug > Trace > Enable Trace and run forward. See the user guide: Debugger > Functions > Backward execution (rewind)

The verb is Step Back or Rewind to frame N, and the reason is read from the machine after the refusal (rewind_refusal_reason() in debugger_control.cpp). The prefix is what the Qt debugger matches to put the reason in its status bar. RefusedCorrupt logs no reason line: the corruption incident is reported on its own.

docs.title: Symbols — CAP-SYM
docs.text:
There is one symbol table, and the backend owns it; the Qt panels, the DSL's @name, the GDB server's monitor sym and --map all read it, so a symbol loaded by one client shows in every other.
